prompt_text:
The figure summarizes how single-cell immune and stromal changes may drive two autoimmune diseases and highlights possible treatment targets.

In systemic lupus erythematosus, the skin, blood, and kidney all show a strong interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) signature across several cell types, including keratinocytes, T cells, plasma cells, monocytes, and dendritic cells. Chemokines such as CCL20, CXCL1, CXCL12, and especially CX3CL1 appear to link tissue inflammation with immune-cell recruitment and activation. In the kidney, tubular cells show increased ISG activity, while resident macrophages and other local cells seem to promote T-cell, B-cell, and myeloid-cell activation. IFNγ-producing CD8 T cells and NK cells are depicted as contributors to chemokine production. The central message is that lupus pathology is broadly interferon driven, with suggested interventions aimed at type I IFN signaling and selected chemokine pathways, and urinary chemokines proposed as biomarkers.

In systemic sclerosis, the emphasis shifts from interferon to fibrosis. The skin shows B-cell accumulation associated with CXCL13, loss of homeostatic fibroblasts, microvascular damage, and emergence of fibroblast states linked to extracellular matrix formation. In the lung, macrophage-derived OPN/SPP1 appears to drive myofibroblast differentiation and matrix deposition, while another fibroblast-like population marked by CTHRC1 is associated with invasive remodeling. Overall, the figure contrasts inflammatory interferon networks in lupus with profibrotic stromal remodeling in scleroderma.
